name: Core: IP Connectivity
description: 58 original questions for IP Connectivity (25% of the v1.1 blueprint).
author: CCNA Academy

questions.stem: Refer to the routing table. Which next hop does R1 use for a packet destined to 10.1.5.20?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show ip route
Codes: C - connected, S - static, O - OSPF, L - local, * - candidate default

Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 9 subnets, 5 masks
C        10.0.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.0.12.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
C        10.0.13.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
L        10.0.13.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
C        10.0.14.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
L        10.0.14.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
O        10.1.0.0/16 [110/20] via 10.0.12.2, 00:10:11, GigabitEthernet0/1
O        10.1.4.0/22 [110/30] via 10.0.13.3, 00:10:11, GigabitEthernet0/2
S        10.1.5.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.14.4
      203.0.113.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        203.0.113.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        203.0.113.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
questions.explanation: The router always picks the longest matching prefix first. Administrative distance only matters between routes to the same prefix.
questions.whyCorrect: The static route 10.1.5.0/24 is the longest prefix that matches 10.1.5.20.
whyWrong: 10.1.4.0/22 also matches, but /24 is more specific.
10.1.0.0/16 matches but is less specific.
The default route is used only when nothing more specific matches.

questions.stem: Refer to the routing table. Which destinations does R1 forward to next hop 10.0.13.3? (Choose two.)
questions.exhibit:
R1# show ip route
Codes: C - connected, S - static, O - OSPF, L - local, * - candidate default

Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 9 subnets, 5 masks
C        10.0.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.0.12.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
C        10.0.13.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
L        10.0.13.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
C        10.0.14.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
L        10.0.14.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
O        10.1.0.0/16 [110/20] via 10.0.12.2, 00:10:11, GigabitEthernet0/1
O        10.1.4.0/22 [110/30] via 10.0.13.3, 00:10:11, GigabitEthernet0/2
S        10.1.5.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.14.4
      203.0.113.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        203.0.113.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        203.0.113.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
questions.explanation: A /22 has a block size of 4 in the third octet: 10.1.4.0/22 covers third-octet values 4–7. More specific routes inside it (10.1.5.0/24) take precedence.
questions.whyCorrect: 10.1.4.0/22 (10.1.4.0–10.1.7.255) is the longest match. Still inside 10.1.4.0/22, and no longer prefix covers it.
whyWrong: The more specific static 10.1.5.0/24 wins, so it goes to 10.0.14.4.
Outside the /22, so only 10.1.0.0/16 matches (via 10.0.12.2).
This is a connected address on Gi0/2, delivered directly.

questions.stem: Refer to the routing table. How does R1 forward a packet destined to 10.2.0.1?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show ip route
Codes: C - connected, S - static, O - OSPF, L - local, * - candidate default

Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 9 subnets, 5 masks
C        10.0.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.0.12.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
C        10.0.13.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
L        10.0.13.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
C        10.0.14.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
L        10.0.14.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
O        10.1.0.0/16 [110/20] via 10.0.12.2, 00:10:11, GigabitEthernet0/1
O        10.1.4.0/22 [110/30] via 10.0.13.3, 00:10:11, GigabitEthernet0/2
S        10.1.5.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.14.4
      203.0.113.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        203.0.113.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        203.0.113.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
questions.explanation: A route matches only if the destination is inside its prefix. When nothing else matches, the default route (0.0.0.0/0) is used.
options: Via 10.0.12.2, because 10.1.0.0/16 is the closest match
Via Gi0/1 as a connected route
questions.whyCorrect: No 10.2.x.x route exists, so the gateway of last resort is used.
whyWrong: A default route exists, so the packet is forwarded.
10.2.0.1 is not on any connected subnet.

questions.stem: Refer to the routing table. What is the OSPF metric of the route used for 10.1.200.1?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show ip route
Codes: C - connected, S - static, O - OSPF, L - local, * - candidate default

Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 9 subnets, 5 masks
C        10.0.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.0.12.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
C        10.0.13.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
L        10.0.13.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
C        10.0.14.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
L        10.0.14.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
O        10.1.0.0/16 [110/20] via 10.0.12.2, 00:10:11, GigabitEthernet0/1
O        10.1.4.0/22 [110/30] via 10.0.13.3, 00:10:11, GigabitEthernet0/2
S        10.1.5.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.14.4
      203.0.113.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        203.0.113.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        203.0.113.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
questions.explanation: Routing table brackets show [administrative distance/metric]. For OSPF the metric is the total cost to the destination.
questions.whyCorrect: 10.1.200.1 matches only 10.1.0.0/16, shown as [110/20]: AD 110, metric 20.
whyWrong: 110 is the administrative distance, not the metric.
30 belongs to 10.1.4.0/22, which does not contain 10.1.200.1.
[1/0] belongs to the static routes.

questions.stem: In the entry 'O 10.1.4.0/22 [110/30] via 10.0.13.3', what do 110 and 30 represent?
questions.explanation: AD ranks route sources (OSPF = 110); the metric compares routes from the same source (OSPF cost).
questions.whyCorrect: Brackets are [AD/metric].
whyWrong: OSPF does not use hop count, and the order is AD first.
Route age appears separately as hh:mm:ss.
These are not shown in the brackets.

questions.stem: A router learns 172.16.8.0/24 from OSPF and from EIGRP (internal), and also has a static route to 172.16.8.0/24 configured with administrative distance 200. Which route is installed?
questions.explanation: Administrative distance can be changed. A static route with a raised AD is a floating static route that is only installed if better sources disappear.
questions.whyCorrect: For the same prefix, the lowest AD wins: EIGRP 90 < OSPF 110 < static 200.
whyWrong: Its AD was raised to 200, so it is now the least preferred.
OSPF's AD of 110 is higher than EIGRP's 90.
Load balancing happens only between equal routes from the same source.

questions.stem: A router has an OSPF route to 192.168.0.0/16 and a RIP route to 192.168.10.0/24. A packet arrives for 192.168.10.5. Which route is used?
questions.explanation: Routes to different prefixes are not compared by AD. The most specific matching prefix always wins.
options: The RIP route, because /24 is a longer prefix
The OSPF route, because its AD (110) is lower than RIP's (120)
Both routes are used for load sharing
questions.whyCorrect: Longest prefix match is applied before administrative distance.
whyWrong: AD only compares routes to the identical prefix.
The prefixes differ, so the more specific one wins.
More specific routes exist.

questions.stem: Match each route source to its default administrative distance.
questions.explanation: Lower administrative distance means more trusted: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, IS-IS 115, RIP 120, iBGP 200.
questions.whyCorrect: Connected → 0; Static → 1; eBGP → 20; EIGRP (internal) → 90; OSPF → 110; RIP → 120

questions.stem: Arrange the criteria a router uses to choose a route, from first evaluated to last.
questions.explanation: Prefix length decides first. AD resolves ties between different sources for the same prefix; the metric resolves ties within one routing protocol.
questions.whyCorrect: Longest prefix match → Lowest administrative distance → Lowest metric

questions.stem: True or false: When a router forwards an IPv4 packet, it decrements the TTL and builds a new Layer 2 header for the outgoing link.
questions.explanation: Routing is a per-hop process: the frame is removed, the TTL is decremented (packets with TTL 0 are dropped), and a new frame is built for the next hop.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is true. Routing is a per-hop process: the frame is removed, the TTL is decremented (packets with TTL 0 are dropped), and a new frame is built for the next hop.
whyWrong: The statement is true, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: Refer to the diagram. As the PC sends a packet to the server, which destination MAC address is in the frame leaving the PC?
questions.explanation: Hosts send off-subnet traffic to the default gateway's MAC. Each router builds a new frame for the next link.
questions.whyCorrect: The server is on another subnet, so the PC frames the packet to its default gateway.
whyWrong: The PC cannot reach the server's MAC across routers.
The PC only communicates directly with devices on its own subnet.
Unicast IP traffic uses the gateway's unicast MAC after ARP.

questions.stem: Refer to the diagram. If R1 loses its OSPF route to 10.2.2.0/24, how does it forward traffic to 10.2.2.10?
questions.explanation: The default route catches every destination without a more specific match. Here it also points to R2, so connectivity continues.
options: Using the static default route via 10.0.12.2
It forwards out Gi0/0 toward the PC
It floods the packet out all interfaces
questions.whyCorrect: 0.0.0.0/0 still matches every destination.
whyWrong: A matching default route exists.
No route points to Gi0/0 for 10.2.2.0/24.
Routers do not flood unknown destinations.

questions.stem: What does a routing-table entry with code 'L', such as 'L 10.0.12.1/32', represent?
questions.explanation: IOS installs a connected (C) route for the subnet and a local (L) /32 route for the interface address itself.
questions.whyCorrect: Local routes are /32 host routes for each configured interface address.
whyWrong: Loopback subnets appear as C/L entries too, but L means local, not loopback.
LDP is a label protocol and does not install L routes.
Manual routes appear with code S.

questions.stem: True or false: If OSPF learns two paths to the same prefix with equal cost, the router can install both and load-share traffic.
questions.explanation: Equal-cost multipath (ECMP) is supported by OSPF; IOS installs up to 4 equal-cost paths by default (configurable with maximum-paths).
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is true. Equal-cost multipath (ECMP) is supported by OSPF; IOS installs up to 4 equal-cost paths by default (configurable with maximum-paths).
whyWrong: The statement is true, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: Based on the output, how does the router forward traffic to 10.9.1.1?
questions.explanation: When multiple next hops appear under one prefix with the same [AD/metric], the router shares traffic between them.
options: It load-shares across both next hops
It uses only 10.0.12.2 because it is listed first
It drops the traffic because the routes conflict
questions.whyCorrect: Two equal-cost OSPF paths are installed for 10.9.0.0/16.
whyWrong: Both entries are active paths.
Equal-cost paths are not a conflict.
10.9.0.0/16 matches more specifically.

questions.stem: A router has no default route and receives a packet for a destination that matches no route. What happens?
questions.explanation: Without a matching route, the packet cannot be forwarded. A default route provides a catch-all.
options: The packet is flooded out all interfaces
The router sends an ARP request for the destination
The packet is sent back out the interface it arrived on
questions.whyCorrect: Routers never guess where to forward.
whyWrong: Flooding is a Layer 2 switch behavior.
ARP is only for directly connected subnets.
That would create a loop.

questions.stem: Which command configures an IPv4 default route to next hop 198.51.100.1?
questions.explanation: The default route appears as S* and sets the gateway of last resort.
questions.whyCorrect: Destination 0.0.0.0 with mask 0.0.0.0 matches every address.
whyWrong: A /32 mask would match only 0.0.0.0.
This is not valid IOS syntax.
IOS requires the 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 form.

questions.stem: R1 learns its default route from OSPF. An engineer wants a backup default route through ISP2 at 192.0.2.1 that is used only if the OSPF default disappears. Which command achieves this?
questions.explanation: A floating static route must use an AD higher than the route it backs up.
questions.whyCorrect: AD 115 is higher than OSPF's 110, so it stays inactive while the OSPF route exists.
whyWrong: The default static AD of 1 would replace the OSPF route immediately.
AD 90 is lower than 110, so this would become the primary route.
AD 100 is still lower than 110.

questions.stem: R1 reaches its IPv6 next hop through link-local address FE80::2 on Gi0/1. Which IPv6 default route is valid?
questions.explanation: IPv6 default route = ::/0. Also ensure 'ipv6 unicast-routing' is enabled.
questions.whyCorrect: A link-local next hop must be paired with the exit interface.
whyWrong: Link-local addresses are only unique per link, so IOS needs the interface.
IPv6 routes use 'ipv6 route'.
::/128 is the unspecified address, not a default route.

questions.stem: R1 has 'ip route 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.0.2', and the route appears in its table. Pings from a PC on R1's LAN (192.168.1.0/24) to 10.20.5.5 fail. R2 has no routes other than its connected networks. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Routing must work in both directions. Add a return route on R2 (or a dynamic protocol) for 192.168.1.0/24.
questions.tip: Ping needs a path there AND back.
options: R2 has no route back to 192.168.1.0/24
The static route's AD is too high
The static route mask should be 255.255.255.0
Static routes do not work for ping
questions.whyCorrect: Echo requests reach the destination, but replies cannot be routed back.
whyWrong: AD only matters when competing routes exist.
A /16 correctly covers 10.20.5.5.
ICMP is routed like any other IP packet.

questions.stem: Which statements about IPv4 static routes are true? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Static routes are predictable and create no protocol overhead, but they do not react to failures except through floating backups.
options: A route with a next-hop address is installed only if the next hop is reachable
Static routes automatically adapt when the topology changes
Static routes are advertised to all neighbors by default
questions.whyCorrect: Only connected routes are more trusted. IOS needs a recursive lookup to succeed.
whyWrong: They must be changed manually (unless a floating route takes over).
They are only advertised if redistributed into a routing protocol.

questions.stem: Which command creates a host route to 10.9.9.9 via next hop 10.0.0.2?
questions.explanation: Host routes (/32) are useful for steering traffic for a single server or loopback.
questions.whyCorrect: A /32 mask matches exactly one address.
whyWrong: This mask describes a /24 network.
A 0.0.0.0 mask turns the route into a default route.
'ip host' creates a local name-to-address mapping.

questions.stem: An engineer configures 'ip route 10.50.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.99.9', but it does not appear in 'show ip route'. What is the most likely reason?
questions.explanation: Check that the next hop is on a connected subnet (or reachable via another route).
options: The next hop 10.0.99.9 is not reachable through any existing route
Its administrative distance is too high
Static routes are hidden from 'show ip route'
Static routing must be enabled with a global command
questions.whyCorrect: IOS installs the route only when the recursive lookup succeeds.
whyWrong: There is no competing route, and AD defaults to 1.
Static routes appear with code S.
IPv4 static routing works by default.

questions.stem: True or false: A static route on an Ethernet interface configured with only an exit interface (no next-hop address) makes the router ARP for each destination, relying on the neighboring router's proxy ARP.
questions.explanation: With no next hop, the router treats destinations as directly connected and ARPs for them. Use a next-hop or fully specified route on multi-access links.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is true. With no next hop, the router treats destinations as directly connected and ARPs for them. Use a next-hop or fully specified route on multi-access links.
whyWrong: The statement is true, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: R1 and R2 share a subnet in area 0 but never become OSPF neighbors. Based on the output, what is the cause?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show ip ospf interface g0/0 | include Process|Network|Timer
  Process ID 1, Router ID 1.1.1.1, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 40, Wait 40, Retransmit 5

R2# show ip ospf interface g0/0 | include Process|Network|Timer
  Process ID 20, Router ID 2.2.2.2, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 5, Dead 20, Wait 20, Retransmit 5
questions.explanation: OSPF neighbor requirements: same area, subnet/mask, Hello/Dead timers, authentication and stub flag; unique router IDs; matching MTU to reach Full.
options: The Hello and Dead timers do not match
questions.whyCorrect: Neighbors must agree on Hello (10 vs 5) and Dead (40 vs 20) intervals.
whyWrong: Process IDs are locally significant and need not match.
Router IDs must be unique, so differing is required.
Both show BROADCAST.

questions.stem: Which parameters must match for two OSPFv2 routers to become neighbors? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Matching: area, subnet, timers, authentication, stub flag (and MTU for Full). Unique: router ID. Irrelevant: process ID.
questions.tip: Process ID is local; area must match.
questions.whyCorrect: Both interfaces must be in the same area. Mismatched timers prevent the adjacency.
whyWrong: Process IDs are local to each router.
Router IDs must be different.
Priority only influences the DR/BDR election.

questions.stem: R1 has no 'router-id' command. Its interfaces are Loopback0 1.1.1.1, Loopback1 10.10.10.10, Gi0/0 192.168.100.1 (up) and Gi0/1 172.16.1.1 (up). What is R1's OSPF router ID?
questions.explanation: Router ID order: manual 'router-id' → highest loopback IPv4 → highest active physical IPv4.
questions.whyCorrect: With no manual router ID, the highest loopback IP is preferred over physical interfaces.
whyWrong: Physical interfaces are used only if no loopback exists.
The highest, not the lowest, loopback address is chosen.
It is neither a loopback nor the highest address.

questions.stem: Three routers on one Ethernet segment start OSPF at the same time: R1 (priority 1, RID 3.3.3.3), R2 (priority 10, RID 1.1.1.1) and R3 (priority 0, RID 9.9.9.9). Which router becomes the DR?
questions.explanation: DR election: highest priority, then highest router ID. Priority 0 never becomes DR or BDR.
options: No DR is elected on Ethernet
questions.whyCorrect: The highest interface priority wins; R2's 10 beats R1's 1.
whyWrong: Priority 0 makes a router ineligible, even with the highest router ID.
Router ID is only a tiebreaker when priorities are equal; R1 becomes the BDR.
Broadcast networks elect a DR and BDR.

questions.stem: R2 is the current DR on a LAN. An engineer raises R1's OSPF priority to 255. What happens?
questions.explanation: OSPF DR/BDR election is non-preemptive to avoid instability. Plan priorities before routers come up.
options: R2 remains the DR; elections are not preemptive
R1 immediately becomes the DR on the LAN
R1 immediately becomes the BDR on the LAN
questions.whyCorrect: R1 becomes DR only after a new election, such as when the DR fails or OSPF is restarted.
whyWrong: The DR is not replaced just because a higher priority appears.
The BDR is not preempted either.
Changing priority does not reset the neighbors.

questions.stem: Based on the output from the local router, which statement is true?
questions.exhibit:
R5# show ip ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID   Pri   State           Dead Time   Address     Interface
2.2.2.2         1   FULL/DR         00:00:35    10.1.1.2    Gi0/0
3.3.3.3         1   2WAY/DROTHER    00:00:33    10.1.1.3    Gi0/0
4.4.4.4         1   FULL/BDR        00:00:38    10.1.1.4    Gi0/0
questions.explanation: On broadcast segments, all routers become FULL with the DR and BDR. DROTHER-to-DROTHER neighbors stay in 2-Way.
options: The local router is a DROTHER; this is normal
The local router is the DR
There is an MTU mismatch with 3.3.3.3
questions.whyCorrect: DROTHERs form full adjacencies only with the DR and BDR.
whyWrong: 2WAY between two DROTHERs is the expected final state.
The DR would be FULL with every neighbor.
MTU problems leave neighbors stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE.

questions.stem: With the default OSPF reference bandwidth, what costs do a 1 Gbps and a 10 Gbps interface receive?
questions.explanation: Raise the reference bandwidth on every router (auto-cost reference-bandwidth) so fast links can be distinguished.
questions.whyCorrect: Cost = 100 Mbps / bandwidth, with a minimum of 1, so all links of 100 Mbps or faster cost 1.
whyWrong: That requires a reference bandwidth of 10 Gbps.
These are STP path costs.
OSPF cost is an integer with a minimum of 1.

questions.stem: After 'auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000' is configured, what is the OSPF cost of a 1 Gbps interface?
questions.explanation: The reference-bandwidth value is in Mbps. Configure the same value on all routers so costs stay consistent.
whyWrong: 1 was the cost with the default 100 Mbps reference.
That would require a 100 Gbps reference.
4 is the STP cost for 1 Gbps.

questions.stem: R1 can reach 10.5.5.0/24 through R2 (outgoing link costs 10 then 10) or through R3 (costs 5 then 20). Which path does OSPF install?
questions.explanation: SPF sums the outgoing interface costs along each path and picks the lowest total.
options: Through R3, because its first link is cheaper
Through R3, because it has fewer hops
questions.whyCorrect: 10 + 10 = 20 is lower than 5 + 20 = 25.
whyWrong: OSPF compares total path cost, not the first hop.
20 and 25 are not equal.
Both paths have the same hop count; OSPF uses cost anyway.

questions.stem: Which command enables OSPF in area 0 only on the interface addressed 172.16.10.5/30, and on no other interface in 172.16.10.0/24?
questions.explanation: The OSPF 'network' statement uses a wildcard mask to select interfaces. Alternatively configure 'ip ospf 1 area 0' directly on the interface.
questions.whyCorrect: The wildcard 0.0.0.3 matches only 172.16.10.4–172.16.10.7.
whyWrong: The network command uses a wildcard mask, not a subnet mask.
This matches every interface in 172.16.10.0/24.
The area must be 0, as required.

questions.stem: LAN interface Gi0/2 must be advertised into OSPF, but no OSPF adjacency should ever form on it. Which command achieves this?
questions.explanation: Passive interfaces are best practice on user-facing LANs to prevent rogue OSPF neighbors.
questions.whyCorrect: The subnet is still advertised, but no Hellos are sent or processed on that interface.
whyWrong: Removing the network statement covering Gi0/2 would stop advertising its subnet.
This only prevents DR/BDR election; adjacencies still form.
The interface and its subnet would go down.

questions.stem: True or false: On an interface configured with 'ip ospf network point-to-point', no DR or BDR is elected.
questions.explanation: Point-to-point networks have only two routers, so a DR is unnecessary. Neighbors appear as FULL/ - in 'show ip ospf neighbor'.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is true. Point-to-point networks have only two routers, so a DR is unnecessary. Neighbors appear as FULL/ - in 'show ip ospf neighbor'.
whyWrong: The statement is true, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: Arrange the OSPF neighbor states in the order a new adjacency moves through them.
questions.explanation: Hellos move neighbors from Down to Init and 2-Way; ExStart chooses master/slave; Exchange swaps DBD summaries; Loading requests missing LSAs; Full means synchronized LSDBs.
questions.tip: Don't Invite 2 Extra Exhausted Lazy Friends.
questions.whyCorrect: Down → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full

questions.stem: R1 has a static default route to the ISP. Which OSPF command advertises this default route to the other OSPF routers?
questions.explanation: Add 'always' to advertise the default even if the router has none in its table.
questions.whyCorrect: It injects a default route into OSPF when one exists in R1's routing table.
whyWrong: This redistributes specific static routes; a default route needs default-information originate.
This enables OSPF on all interfaces; it does not advertise a default route.
This is not how OSPF advertises a default route.

questions.stem: Which statement describes how OSPF builds its routes?
questions.explanation: Link-state: share topology (LSAs) → synchronize the LSDB → each router computes shortest paths independently.
options: Each router runs SPF on a shared LSDB
Routers send their full routing tables to neighbors every 30 seconds
Routers choose paths with the fewest hops
The DR calculates the routes for every router on the segment
questions.whyCorrect: OSPF is a link-state protocol.
whyWrong: That describes RIP.
OSPF uses cost, not hop count.
The DR reduces flooding; each router still runs SPF itself.

questions.stem: Match each OSPF item to its value.
questions.explanation: OSPF runs directly over IP (protocol 89), uses 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6, and has AD 110.
questions.whyCorrect: Multicast address for all OSPF routers → 224.0.0.5; Multicast address for DR/BDR → 224.0.0.6; Administrative distance → 110; IP protocol number → 89
left: Multicast address for all OSPF routers

questions.stem: Two OSPF neighbors stay stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE and never reach FULL. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Fix by matching the MTU on both interfaces (or, as a workaround, 'ip ospf mtu-ignore').
options: A passive interface on one side
questions.whyCorrect: Database description packets are rejected when the MTUs differ.
whyWrong: Routers with mismatched areas never get past Init.
Mismatched timers prevent the neighbor from being seen at all.
A passive interface sends no Hellos, so no neighbor appears.

questions.stem: Which command shows, for each OSPF interface, its area, cost, state (DR/BDR/DROTHER/P2P) and neighbor count?
questions.explanation: Use 'show ip ospf interface brief' for interface status, 'show ip ospf neighbor' for adjacencies and 'show ip protocols' for process settings.
questions.whyCorrect: It summarizes OSPF-enabled interfaces with area, cost, state and neighbors.
whyWrong: It lists neighbors, not per-interface cost.
It shows only OSPF-learned routes.
It shows process-level settings such as router ID and passive interfaces.

questions.stem: What problem do first hop redundancy protocols solve?
questions.explanation: HSRP, VRRP and GLBP let two or more routers present one virtual IP/MAC as the hosts' default gateway.
options: They keep the hosts' default gateway available
They balance traffic across WAN links to the internet
questions.whyCorrect: Routers share a virtual IP that stays reachable if one router fails.
whyWrong: That is the job of STP.
FHRPs protect the first hop, not WAN path selection.
DHCP redundancy uses separate mechanisms.

questions.stem: Refer to the diagram. If R1 fails, what must the hosts change to keep reaching other networks?
questions.explanation: The new active router sends gratuitous ARPs so switches update their MAC tables for the virtual MAC.
options: Nothing; R2 takes over the virtual IP
questions.whyCorrect: Hosts keep the same gateway IP and ARP entry.
whyWrong: The virtual IP removes the need to reconfigure hosts.
DHCP is not involved in FHRP failover.
The virtual MAC stays the same, so cached entries remain valid.

questions.stem: Refer to the diagram. When R1 recovers after the failure, will it become the active router again?
questions.explanation: HSRP preemption is off by default and must be enabled with 'standby <group> preempt'.
options: Yes, because of preempt and priority 110
No, because R2 has the higher priority
questions.whyCorrect: Preemption lets the higher-priority router reclaim the active role.
whyWrong: HSRP supports preemption, but it must be configured.
100 is lower than 110.
Preemption does not require reloading R2.

questions.stem: Match each description to its first hop redundancy protocol.
questions.explanation: HSRP and GLBP are Cisco protocols; VRRP is the open standard. Only GLBP natively load-balances among gateways.
questions.whyCorrect: Cisco proprietary; active and standby routers → HSRP; IETF standard; master and backup routers → VRRP; Cisco proprietary; multiple routers forward at once using different virtual MACs → GLBP
left: Cisco proprietary; active and standby routers
IETF standard; master and backup routers
Cisco proprietary; multiple routers forward at once using different virtual MACs

questions.stem: True or false: HSRP preemption is enabled by default.
questions.explanation: HSRP preemption must be configured; VRRP enables preemption by default.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is false. HSRP preemption must be configured; VRRP enables preemption by default.
whyWrong: The statement is false, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: Which routing protocol is a path-vector protocol used between autonomous systems on the internet?
questions.explanation: IGPs (OSPF, EIGRP, RIP, IS-IS) route within an organization; BGP routes between autonomous systems.
questions.whyCorrect: BGP exchanges reachability with AS-path information between autonomous systems.
whyWrong: OSPF is a link-state interior gateway protocol.
RIP is a distance-vector IGP using hop count.
EIGRP is an advanced distance-vector IGP.

questions.stem: Refer to the IPv6 routing table. Which next hop does R1 use for 2001:DB8:10:5::77?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show ipv6 route
O   2001:DB8:10::/48 [110/20]
     via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/1
S   2001:DB8:10:5::/64 [1/0]
     via 2001:DB8:FF::3
C   2001:DB8:FF::/64 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/2, directly connected
L   2001:DB8:FF::1/128 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/2, receive
S   ::/0 [1/0]
     via 2001:DB8:FF::9
questions.explanation: Longest prefix match works the same way for IPv6. The fourth hextet (5) places the address inside 2001:DB8:10:5::/64.
options: The packet is delivered directly out Gi0/2
questions.whyCorrect: The static /64 is the longest prefix containing the destination.
whyWrong: The OSPF /48 also matches, but /64 is more specific.
The default route is used only when nothing else matches.
2001:DB8:10:5::/64 is not a connected prefix.

questions.stem: Refer to the IPv6 routing table. Which destinations are forwarded to FE80::2? (Choose two.)
questions.exhibit:
R1# show ipv6 route
O   2001:DB8:10::/48 [110/20]
     via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/1
S   2001:DB8:10:5::/64 [1/0]
     via 2001:DB8:FF::3
C   2001:DB8:FF::/64 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/2, directly connected
L   2001:DB8:FF::1/128 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/2, receive
S   ::/0 [1/0]
     via 2001:DB8:FF::9
questions.explanation: A /48 fixes the first three hextets (2001:DB8:10); any value in the fourth hextet matches unless a longer prefix exists.
questions.whyCorrect: Inside the /48 and not covered by the more specific static /64. Still inside 2001:DB8:10::/48 (the fourth hextet can be 0–FFFF).
whyWrong: The static 2001:DB8:10:5::/64 is more specific.
The third hextet 11 is outside the /48, so the default route is used.

questions.stem: In 'show ip route', what does the code 'O IA' indicate?
questions.explanation: CCNA configuration focuses on single-area OSPF, but you should still recognize O, O IA and O E2 in routing tables.
options: An OSPF inter-area route learned from another area
An OSPF route inside the router's own area
An external route redistributed into OSPF
questions.whyCorrect: IA routes come from summary LSAs created by an ABR.
whyWrong: Intra-area routes are shown with just 'O'.
External routes are shown as O E1 or O E2.
Inactive routes are not shown in the routing table.

questions.stem: R1 uses 'network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0'. R2's connected interface 10.0.12.2/30 uses 'ip ospf 1 area 1'. Both processes are otherwise correct. Will they become neighbors?
questions.explanation: The two configuration methods are equivalent; what matters is that both sides place the link in the same area.
options: No, because the area IDs do not match
Yes, because the network statement and interface command are interchangeable
No, because one router uses a network statement and the other uses an interface command
questions.whyCorrect: Hellos carry the area ID, and mismatched areas are rejected.
whyWrong: They are interchangeable, but the areas still differ.
Process IDs never need to match; areas do.
Mixing methods works fine.

questions.stem: 'show ip ospf neighbor' shows neighbor 2.2.2.2 in state 'FULL/ -' on Gi0/1. What does the dash mean?
questions.explanation: Serial links and Ethernet links set to 'ip ospf network point-to-point' show FULL/- neighbors.
options: The link is point-to-point, so there is no DR/BDR
The neighbor's priority is 0 on a broadcast network
questions.whyCorrect: Point-to-point links do not elect a DR.
whyWrong: FULL means the adjacency is complete.
DROTHERs appear as DROTHER.
It would show FULL/DROTHER or 2WAY/DROTHER.

questions.stem: R1 has 'ip route 10.70.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.12.2' and 'ip route 10.70.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.13.3'. Both next hops are reachable. What does the routing table contain?
questions.explanation: Equal static routes provide simple load sharing. Give one a higher AD to make it a floating backup instead.
options: Both static routes, and traffic is load-shared across them
Only the first route that was configured
Only the route with the lower next-hop address
questions.whyCorrect: Equal prefix, AD and metric → both are installed.
whyWrong: IOS installs equal static routes together.
Next-hop address is not a tiebreaker.
Parallel static routes are valid.

questions.stem: R1 has 'ipv6 route ::/0 2001:DB8:1::1' and 'ipv6 route ::/0 2001:DB8:2::1 200'. Both next hops are reachable. Which route is used?
questions.explanation: The floating route is installed only if the primary route disappears, for example when its next hop becomes unreachable.
options: Neither, because IPv6 does not support floating routes
questions.whyCorrect: It has the default AD of 1; the other is a floating route with AD 200.
whyWrong: AD 200 is less preferred.
Their ADs differ, so only one is installed.
Floating static routes work for IPv6 too.

questions.stem: HSRP group 10 has no preempt configured. R2 (priority 100) is active. R1 (priority 120) boots and joins the group. Which router is active?
questions.explanation: Configure preempt on the router that should always be active, usually with a delay so routing can converge first.
options: Neither; an election restarts and traffic stops
questions.whyCorrect: Without preemption, a higher-priority router does not take over an established active router.
whyWrong: That requires 'standby 10 preempt' on R1.
HSRP has exactly one active router per group.
A router joining does not interrupt the active router.

questions.stem: Refer to the routing table. An engineer adds 'ip route 10.1.4.0 255.255.252.0 10.0.14.4'. What happens to traffic for 10.1.6.1?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show ip route
Codes: C - connected, S - static, O - OSPF, L - local, * - candidate default

Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 9 subnets, 5 masks
C        10.0.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.0.12.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
C        10.0.13.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
L        10.0.13.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
C        10.0.14.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
L        10.0.14.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
O        10.1.0.0/16 [110/20] via 10.0.12.2, 00:10:11, GigabitEthernet0/1
O        10.1.4.0/22 [110/30] via 10.0.13.3, 00:10:11, GigabitEthernet0/2
S        10.1.5.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.14.4
      203.0.113.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        203.0.113.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        203.0.113.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
questions.explanation: When two sources offer exactly the same prefix, only the lowest-AD route is installed. The OSPF route remains in the OSPF database as a backup.
options: It still goes to 10.0.13.3, because OSPF learned the route first
It goes to the default route
questions.whyCorrect: Same prefix, so the lower AD wins.
whyWrong: Learning order does not matter.
Routes with different ADs are not combined.
A /22 route still matches.

questions.stem: An engineer enters 'router-id 5.5.5.5' under a running OSPF process, but 'show ip protocols' still shows the old router ID. Why?
questions.explanation: Changing the router ID resets adjacencies, so plan it during a maintenance window.
options: The OSPF process must be restarted
Router IDs must match a loopback address
Manual router IDs are ignored when a loopback exists
The router ID can only be changed by removing the network statements
questions.whyCorrect: IOS warns that a reload or process clear is required.
whyWrong: Any unique 32-bit value is allowed.
A manual router-id always has the highest preference.
Only a process restart is required.
